cuisines.name: American
cuisines.notes: - Meatloaf → Hawaiian Mac Salad (classic diner starch) or Gochujang Green Beans (rhymes with the sriracha-ketchup glaze) - High Protein Meatballs → Gochujang Green Beans; both hold up for meal prep - Chick-fil-A Chicken Sandwich → Hawaiian Mac Salad; the deli pairing for fried chicken - Ground Beef Tacos → Ensalada de Elote (Mexican Street Corn Salad); corn salad alongside a taco spread, the same pairing the Mexican braises take The meatballs and meatloaf are seasoned neutrally enough to take a bolder side than their cuisine would suggest. The sandwich arrives complete — pickles and bun included — so anything alongside it is optional.

cuisines.name: Argentine
cuisines.notes: Chimichurri is herbs, vinegar, and olive oil — carb-free without modification. Make it ahead; it wants at least 30 minutes to come together.

cuisines.name: Brazilian
cuisines.notes: Churrasco tradition seasons picanha with coarse salt and nothing else, which makes it accidentally ideal keto food. The fat cap is the whole point — don't let anyone trim it.

cuisines.name: Chinese
cuisines.notes: Char siu is a component as much as a dish — served over rice, sliced into noodle soups, tucked into bao, or (per the recipe's own note) rolled into egg rolls. Traditionally it comes with plain steamed rice and a simple green vegetable — gai lan or bok choy. Neither is in the vault, so the Korean banchan stand in: Sigeumchi Namul (Spinach Banchan) covers the green, and Oi Muchim (Cucumber Salad) the acid. A plain blanched Chinese green would be the more authentic addition. The marinade leans on specialty ingredients — red fermented bean curd, Chinese rose wine, maltose, red yeast rice — that are worth sourcing once and keeping. The sous vide version skips all of them for supermarket staples (hoisin, honey, Shaoxing or sherry) and is the better make-ahead option.

cuisines.name: Creole
cuisines.notes: Earthy and deeply spiced. One good match in the vault: - Hawaiian Mac Salad — a creamy, cooling starch salad; the Southern potluck pairing with Cajun rice dishes

cuisines.name: Ethiopian
cuisines.notes: Doro wat is normally scooped up with injera, which is off the table on keto — this version is served over sautéed cabbage or cauliflower rice instead. The onion base is where the carbs live, and the recipe already uses fewer onions than tradition calls for.

cuisines.name: Filipino
cuisines.notes: A complete one-pan dish. Can be served as-is or with a light side like Gochujang Green Beans for added color and freshness.

cuisines.name: French
cuisines.notes: Bourguignon is served over mashed potatoes and needs nothing else. Mussels want crusty bread for the broth. This gap has closed. These recipes used to have no compatible side — the vault's sides were all Korean or Hawaiian, none of which belong next to a red-wine braise. The keto collection changed that: - Sauteed Spinach with Garlic and Lemon — the simple green all three want - Grilled Asparagus with Lemon and Parmesan — especially with the steak - Tomato Cucumber Feta Salad — the light salad the mussels were missing

cuisines.name: Greek
cuisines.notes: Tzatziki is the connective tissue across the whole collection, not just this hub — the souvlaki, the smoked leg of lamb, the smoked wings, and the fast-smoked thighs all call for it. Worth making a batch at the start of a grilling week. Smoked Butterflied Leg of Lamb is filed here rather than under American despite sharing a kettle and a technique with the smoked chicken and pork: the lemon-garlic-oregano rub and the tzatziki alongside make it a Greek dish that happens to be smoked, where the others are American smokes that happen to be seasoned Mediterranean. The two salads look redundant and aren't. Classic Greek Salad is the full horiatiki with slab feta, meant to stand on its own; the chopped version is smaller and faster, and its juices work as a sauce for grilled meat.

cuisines.name: Hawaiian
cuisines.notes: The two work quite differently, despite sharing a cuisine tag: - Hawaiian Slaw is soy, sesame, and ginger — effectively an East Asian side. Good with Teriyaki Chicken; wrong next to European or Latin mains. - Hawaiian Mac Salad is a plain creamy starch salad, so it travels much further: Meatloaf, Mushroom Jambalaya, and most American comfort food.

cuisines.name: Indian
cuisines.notes: All are rich and heavily spiced. The two butter chickens include their own starch; Vindaloo wants rice or naan. Two butter chickens. Butter Chicken with Rice is the clipped original, which blends butternut squash and cauliflower into the sauce and serves over rice. Keto Butter Chicken is the aigenerated version — a more orthodox murgh makhani with the sugar left out, over cauliflower rice. Different enough to justify keeping both. The Korean banchan still clash with everything here. But Herbed Cauliflower Rice Pilaf now covers the starch these curries need, and Sauteed Spinach with Garlic and Lemon works as a simple green — both arrived with the keto collection. A cooling raita is still the real gap, especially for Vindaloo.

cuisines.name: Italian
cuisines.notes: The dough recipe feeds the pizza recipe. Both use authentic Neapolitan techniques and extended fermentation for maximum flavor. No side needed — a margherita is complete on its own. The four low-carb entries come from aigenerated Mediterranean-keto set and are Italian by preparation rather than by that collection's theme: capers and white wine, acqua pazza, pesto, parmesan. Grilled Asparagus with Lemon and Parmesan is the one side here, and it suits the grilled mains across the collection more than it suits pizza.

cuisines.name: Jamaican
cuisines.notes: Traditional jerk marinades lean on brown sugar; here allspice, clove, and cinnamon carry the warmth instead. Pimento wood is traditional and hard to find — oak or pecan is the practical substitute. Another kettle smoke, so see American for the rest of that group.

cuisines.name: Japanese
cuisines.notes: Quick, bright, and glossy. The vault's best-served main — its soy/mirin base sits comfortably next to the Korean banchan: - Sigeumchi Namul (Spinach Banchan) — sesame spinach, a natural teriyaki side - Hawaiian Slaw — its ginger, soy, and sesame echo the glaze

cuisines.name: Korean
cuisines.notes: The fried chicken is the vault's first Korean main, and it gives the banchan somewhere to go — it's served as a spread, with cucumber, kimchi, and pickles improvised inline. The dedicated banchan notes above are fuller versions of those same steps, so reach for them instead. The banchan remain the vault's largest side category, but their gochujang/doenjang/sesame base means they don't cross over to European, Indian, or Latin mains. Pair within East Asian dishes, or with neutrally-seasoned proteins.

cuisines.name: Levantine
cuisines.notes: Served as a bowl rather than wrapped in pita, with tahini standing in as both sauce and fat source. Like the Moroccan chermoula, this is genuinely Mediterranean in the dietary sense as well as the geographic one.

cuisines.name: Mediterranean
cuisines.notes: Herbed Cauliflower Rice Pilaf and Sauteed Spinach with Garlic and Lemon are the two workhorse sides for the whole Mediterranean-keto collection, not just this hub — they're what the Greek and Italian mains reach for when they call for "cauliflower rice or a green." Keto Shakshuka with Feta is the loosest fit here in two senses: its tomatoes make it the least strictly keto of the set, and as a North African dish it's the one entry that might deserve its own cuisine rather than the regional label.

cuisines.name: Mexican
cuisines.notes: Both mains are self-contained taco fillings, arriving with their own accompaniments — Birria with tortillas, onion, coriander, and lime; Carnitas with salsa verde, quick-pickled red onions, and cilantro. Neither needs a side. Ensalada de Elote (Mexican Street Corn Salad) is nonetheless a genuine match for either, and the vault's first honest cross-recipe pairing: grilled corn salad next to a taco spread is a standard combination, not a stretch. Birria and the carnitas are close cousins — long low braises of a tough cut, shredded into tortillas. Birria is chile-forward with a consommé for dipping; carnitas is citrus-and-cinnamon with a crisped exterior. Two carnitas recipes now. Carnitas (Tacos) is the clipped original, with salsa verde and pickled onions built in. Pork Carnitas is the aigenerated keto rewrite — same braise-then-crisp method, but citrus zest replaces the orange and milk, and it's served over slaw or in lettuce cups. Keep both or drop one; they're not meaningfully different in technique.

cuisines.name: Moroccan
cuisines.notes: Chermoula is the point here and it keeps — the recipe suggests making extra and using it on chicken or vegetables through the week. It's carb-free as written, and one of the few dishes in the keto collection that also earns diet/mediterranean on its own merits.

cuisines.name: Peruvian
cuisines.notes: Pollo a la brasa flavors adapted to a kettle. The aji verde — cilantro, jalapeño, mayo, lime — is what makes the dish and needs no keto adjustment. Same two-zone setup as the other kettle smokes; see American for those.

cuisines.name: Thai
cuisines.notes: Rich with coconut milk, and traditionally served with pickled mustard greens, shallots, and lime. Oi Muchim (Cucumber Salad) fills that acid-and-crunch role closely enough to work.

cuisines.name: Vietnamese
cuisines.notes: The banh mi is self-contained — pickled daikon and carrot, cucumber, jalapeño, cilantro, and nuoc cham are all built into the sandwich. No side needed. Its components are the useful part to keep around: the do chua holds for 90 days and the nuoc cham for a month, so both are worth making in advance of any Vietnamese cooking.

recipes.title: Authentic Neapolitan Pizza Dough
recipes.summary: Classic long-fermented Neapolitan pizza dough made by hand, following the step-by-step "Neapolitan Pizza From Scratch" video series from mypizzacorner.com. Mixed by hand, bulk proved ~20 hours, then balled and proved again before shaping. Source: Authentic Neapolitan Pizza Recipe Want to scale this to a different number of pizzas or dough weight? Use the Pizza Dough Calculator (set Type of Pizza to "Neapolitan").

steps.md: Add water to the bowl first.

steps.text: Add the flour on top of the water.
steps.md: Add the flour on top of the water.

steps.text: Put the salt on one side of the flour, the yeast on the opposite side (keeps the salt from killing the yeast on contact).
steps.md: Put the salt on one side of the flour, the yeast on the opposite side (keeps the salt from killing the yeast on contact).

steps.text: Cup your hand with fingers together, no gaps.
steps.md: Cup your hand with fingers together, no gaps.

steps.text: Mix in circular motions, starting from the center of the bowl and working outward.
steps.md: Mix in circular motions, starting from the center of the bowl and working outward.

steps.text: Keep mixing until a shaggy dough forms.
steps.md: Keep mixing until a shaggy dough forms.

steps.text: Press down firmly with the heel of your hand to pick up any remaining loose flour.
steps.md: Press down firmly with the heel of your hand to pick up any remaining loose flour.

steps.text: Transfer to a clean bowl and cover with cling film.
steps.md: Transfer to a clean bowl and cover with cling film.

steps.text: Rest 10–60 minutes (autolyse) — it will look dry/shaggy now, that's expected; it softens as the flour hydrates.
steps.md: Rest 10–60 minutes (autolyse) — it will look dry/shaggy now, that's expected; it softens as the flour hydrates.
sub: From the video:

steps.text: 00 flour and strong bread flour both work because they're similar protein content (~12%) — bread flour just needs a bit more water (see substitute quantities above).
steps.md: 00 flour and strong bread flour both work because they're similar protein content (~12%) — bread flour just needs a bit more water (see substitute quantities above).

steps.text: Use cold or room-temp water only — hot water can damage the yeast.
steps.md: Use cold or room-temp water only — hot water can damage the yeast.

steps.text: Prefer instant dried yeast over active dried; active dried needs a 10–15 min pre-mix with water to activate before it goes in the dough.
steps.md: Prefer instant dried yeast over active dried; active dried needs a 10–15 min pre-mix with water to activate before it goes in the dough.

steps.text: Because the yeast quantity is so tiny for a 24h proof, use a scale accurate to 0.01g just for the yeast (a separate cheap scale from your main kitchen scale). If in doubt, err slightly over rather than under on yeast — an over-proofed dough can be rescued by "knocking back" (deflating and letting it re-rise), but an under-proofed one can't be fixed.
steps.md: Because the yeast quantity is so tiny for a 24h proof, use a scale accurate to 0.01g just for the yeast (a separate cheap scale from your main kitchen scale). If in doubt, err slightly over rather than under on yeast — an over-proofed dough can be rescued by "knocking back" (deflating and letting it re-rise), but an under-proofed one can't be fixed.

steps.text: This is intentionally a fairly dry/stiff dough at the mixing stage — that's what gives Neapolitan dough the strength to stretch thin without tearing.
steps.md: This is intentionally a fairly dry/stiff dough at the mixing stage — that's what gives Neapolitan dough the strength to stretch thin without tearing.

steps.text: After the rest, pin the near edge of the dough to the counter with your non-dominant hand.
steps.md: After the rest, pin the near edge of the dough to the counter with your non-dominant hand.

steps.text: Press down on the far side with the heel of your other hand, stretching it away from you.
steps.md: Press down on the far side with the heel of your other hand, stretching it away from you.

steps.text: Roll the dough back up with your fingers while stretching the middle.
steps.md: Roll the dough back up with your fingers while stretching the middle.

steps.text: Turn the dough 45° and repeat.
steps.md: Turn the dough 45° and repeat.

steps.text: Continue for about 4–5 minutes total — it becomes easier to work as the gluten develops.
steps.md: Continue for about 4–5 minutes total — it becomes easier to work as the gluten develops.

steps.text: Cover and rest another 30 minutes before testing.
steps.md: Cover and rest another 30 minutes before testing.
sub: From the video: hearing small bubbles pop as you knead is a good sign — it means air is being worked into the dough, which helps the rise and crumb later. Hand-kneading (vs. a stand mixer) is recommended, partly because it's harder to over-knead by hand and partly because you build an intuitive feel for the dough's texture.

steps.text: This test is optional — skip it once you're confident your kneading is consistently good.
steps.md: This test is optional — skip it once you're confident your kneading is consistently good.

steps.md: Let the dough rest ~30 minutes after kneading first; it's too tense to test accurately right after kneading.

steps.text: Stretch a small piece of dough thin between your fingers.
steps.md: Stretch a small piece of dough thin between your fingers.

steps.text: If it stretches into a translucent "windowpane" without tearing, gluten development is sufficient — move on to the bulk prove.
steps.md: If it stretches into a translucent "windowpane" without tearing, gluten development is sufficient — move on to the bulk prove.

steps.text: Cover the dough (kept in one lump) and leave at room temperature for ~18–20 hours (8 hours minimum, 24 hours is ideal for the best flavor/texture).
steps.md: Cover the dough (kept in one lump) and leave at room temperature for **~18–20 hours** (8 hours minimum, 24 hours is ideal for the best flavor/texture).

steps.text: Cover with cling film, a loosely tied plastic bag, or a lid — avoid a damp cloth for a prove this long, since it dries out and lets the dough form a skin over that many hours.
steps.md: Cover with cling film, a loosely tied plastic bag, or a lid — avoid a damp cloth for a prove this long, since it dries out and lets the dough form a skin over that many hours.

steps.text: Don't divide/ball the dough right after kneading — a long bulk prove in one piece is more forgiving than proving pre-balled portions, and it's easier to "knock back" (deflate and let it re-rise) a bulk mass if it's proving faster than expected.

steps.text: Time this for 4–6 hours before you plan to cook — not right after the bulk prove finishes, or the shaped balls will lose their strength/shape over a long final wait.
steps.md: Time this for **4–6 hours before you plan to cook** — not right after the bulk prove finishes, or the shaped balls will lose their strength/shape over a long final wait.

steps.text: Turn the dough out without adding any flour or water — you want to keep it exactly as is.
steps.md: Turn the dough out without adding any flour or water — you want to keep it exactly as is.

steps.text: Divide the dough into four 250g portions by tearing/weighing on a scale (doesn't need to be exact, ±a few grams is fine).

steps.text: Build tension by folding each portion several times on the bench or in your hands, then round it off — or, faster: tuck the edges under with your fingers and squeeze/rotate it through your fingers into a tight ball.

A bowl makes it hard to get a dough scraper underneath to release the ball later without deflating it (degassing); a flat-bottomed box lets you slide a scraper/wallpaper-scraper under it cleanly. extras.heading: Notes & Troubleshooting
extras.md:
- **Hydration:** this recipe runs about 56% hydration, which is lower than many recipes (60–62%+). Lower hydration is easier to shape and more forgiving for beginners; once you're comfortable, you can work up to a wetter, more open-crumb dough.
- **Salt:** roughly 2–2.5% of the flour's weight.
- **Yeast troubleshooting:** slightly too much yeast is recoverable (knock the dough back and let it re-prove); too little yeast generally isn't — if in doubt, err a touch high.
- **Timing is flexible:** initial rest before kneading can be anywhere from 10 minutes to 1 hour; balling should happen 4–6 hours before cooking, not immediately after the bulk prove.

extras.heading: Ingredients
extras.md:
### Dough (yields 4 pizzas)
| Ingredient | Amount |
|------------|--------|

| Ingredient | Amount |
|------------|--------|

|------------|--------|

extras.heading: Tips
extras.md:
- Water temperature is critical—too cold and dough won't ferment enough; too warm and it will over-proof
- Bread flour can substitute for 00 flour but won't be as tender
- Pop ALL large bubbles before and during shaping—they will burn at high heat
- Don't cut too soon; let cool 1 minute or cheese will slide off
- Pizza is best in the 3-5 minute window after coming out of the oven

extras.heading: General Sentiment
extras.md: The recipe creator emphasizes that Neapolitan pizza has "the potential to be the best bite of pizza you'll ever have" when done right, but warns the sweet spot is very small—anything outside it is "aggressively mid." The long fermentation and precise technique are designed to hit that perfect balance of flavor, texture, and char.

recipes.title: Pizza Dough Calculator
recipes.summary: An interactive dough calculator, rebuilt in Obsidian using a dataviewjs code block (needs the Dataview plugin with JavaScript queries enabled: Settings → Dataview → Enable JavaScript Queries). Modeled on the logic behind the mypizzacorner.com dough calculator — same overall approach (baker's percentages for flour/water/salt, plus a temperature- and time-adjusted yeast estimate), reimplemented independently below rather than embedded from the site.

extras.heading: How it works
Notes
extras.md:
- **Pizza type** sets the default hydration range (Neapolitan 55–62%, New York 60–70%, Detroit/focaccia 70–80%) — pick your style first, then fine-tune hydration within its range.
- **Cold proof** locks you to a "Long" proof length and a fixed fridge temperature band, matching how a real cold retard is normally run (24–48h at ~4–7°C).
- The yeast amount is always an *estimate* — flour brand, exact room temperature, and how active your yeast is will shift the real number. Treat it as a solid starting point, not gospel, especially the first few times you make a given style.
- See [[Authentic Neapolitan Pizza Dough]] for the full hand-mixing method this calculator's Neapolitan defaults pair with.

steps.text: Pat the wings very dry. Toss with salt, baking powder, garlic powder, paprika, and pepper. For best skin, refrigerate uncovered overnight; otherwise proceed.
steps.md: Pat the wings very dry. Toss with salt, baking powder, garlic powder, paprika, and pepper. For best skin, refrigerate uncovered overnight; otherwise proceed.

steps.text: Run the kettle two-zone at 325°F — hotter than a typical smoke on purpose — with one wood chunk.
steps.md: Run the kettle two-zone at 325°F — hotter than a typical smoke on purpose — with one wood chunk.

steps.text: Smoke the wings indirect about 60–75 minutes, flipping once, until 185°F and the skin is rendered and golden. Finish 2–3 minutes over direct heat if you want more crisp.

recipes.title: Sous Vide Char Siu (Chinese BBQ Pork)
recipes.summary: A tender, flavorful char siu made easy with sous vide cooking. The extended low-temperature cook renders collagen for perfectly juicy pork without it falling apart, while a quick broil with honey glaze creates that signature mahogany char. Serve in steamed buns or over rice.

items.name: Shaoxing Chinese rice wine or dry sherry

steps.name: Make marinade
steps.text: Whisk soy sauce, sugar, hoisin, rice wine, ginger, sesame oil, garlic, food coloring (if using), five-spice powder, and pepper together. Reserve 1 cup marinade in refrigerator. Whisk pink curing salt (if using) into remaining marinade.
steps.md: Whisk soy sauce, sugar, hoisin, rice wine, ginger, sesame oil, garlic, food coloring (if using), five-spice powder, and pepper together. Reserve 1 cup marinade in refrigerator. Whisk pink curing salt (if using) into remaining marinade.

steps.name: Marinate pork
steps.text: Trim pork and slice crosswise into ¾-inch-thick steaks. Add to marinade, toss to coat, cover, and refrigerate 10-16 hours.
steps.md: Trim pork and slice crosswise into ¾-inch-thick steaks. Add to marinade, toss to coat, cover, and refrigerate 10-16 hours.

steps.name: Sous vide
steps.text: Heat water to 149°F/65°C. Remove steaks from marinade, divide between two 1-gallon zipper-lock bags, seal removing air, and submerge. Cook 12-16 hours.
steps.md: Heat water to 149°F/65°C. Remove steaks from marinade, divide between two 1-gallon zipper-lock bags, seal removing air, and submerge. Cook 12-16 hours.

steps.name: Make glaze
steps.text: Whisk honey with reserved marinade in saucepan. Cook over medium heat until reduced to about 1 cup, 4-8 minutes.
steps.md: Whisk honey with reserved marinade in saucepan. Cook over medium heat until reduced to about 1 cup, 4-8 minutes.

steps.name: Broil
steps.text: Position rack 6 inches from broiler. Place steaks on wire rack set in foil-lined baking sheet. Pat dry, brush with half the glaze, and broil 2-6 minutes per side until mahogany. Brush with remaining glaze and broil until dark mahogany and lightly charred, 2-6 minutes.
steps.md: Position rack 6 inches from broiler. Place steaks on wire rack set in foil-lined baking sheet. Pat dry, brush with half the glaze, and broil 2-6 minutes per side until mahogany. Brush with remaining glaze and broil until dark mahogany and lightly charred, 2-6 minutes.

steps.name: Rest and serve
steps.text: Transfer to cutting board, let rest 10 minutes, then slice crosswise into ½-inch strips.
steps.md: Transfer to cutting board, let rest 10 minutes, then slice crosswise into ½-inch strips.

recipes.title: Teriyaki Chicken
recipes.summary: Pan-seared chicken thighs finished in a glossy homemade teriyaki sauce built from mirin, soy sauce, and a touch of sake.

steps.name: Season
steps.text: Season the chicken thighs with salt and black pepper — go easy on the salt, since the soy sauce will add more seasoning later.
steps.md: Season the chicken thighs with salt and black pepper — go easy on the salt, since the soy sauce will add more seasoning later.

steps.name: Sear
steps.text: Add vegetable oil to a hot pan (induction 8). Once the oil is shimmering, add the chicken thighs in one even layer, searing in batches if needed to avoid crowding the pan.
steps.md: Add vegetable oil to a hot pan (induction 8). Once the oil is shimmering, add the chicken thighs in one even layer, searing in batches if needed to avoid crowding the pan.

steps.text: Once the chicken thighs are well browned on both sides (they don't need to be fully cooked yet), remove them from the pan and set aside to rest.
steps.md: Once the chicken thighs are well browned on both sides (they don't need to be fully cooked yet), remove them from the pan and set aside to rest.

steps.name: Cook the aromatics
steps.text: Reduce the heat to medium-high (induction 7), skim off any excess fat, then add the sliced onion and ginger to the pan. Stir frequently to prevent burning and cook until the onions are slightly browned.
steps.md: Reduce the heat to medium-high (induction 7), skim off any excess fat, then add the sliced onion and ginger to the pan. Stir frequently to prevent burning and cook until the onions are slightly browned.

steps.name: Build the sauce
steps.text: Add the mirin and cook until it reduces to a syrupy texture. Add a dash of sake and cook until the alcohol has mostly evaporated, then add the soy sauce and cook for another minute.
steps.md: Add the mirin and cook until it reduces to a syrupy texture. Add a dash of sake and cook until the alcohol has mostly evaporated, then add the soy sauce and cook for another minute.

steps.name: Finish the chicken
steps.text: Return the chicken thighs to the pan and cook, basting frequently with the sauce, until fully cooked (74°C / 165°F or above) and the sauce has reduced to your desired thickness.
steps.md: Return the chicken thighs to the pan and cook, basting frequently with the sauce, until fully cooked (74°C / 165°F or above) and the sauce has reduced to your desired thickness.

steps.name: Serve
steps.text: Carve the chicken thighs and pass the sauce through a sieve, reducing it further to a glaze if desired. Spoon the sauce over the chicken and serve.

recipes.title: White Wine Steamed Mussels
recipes.summary: This elegant yet simple dish features fresh mussels steamed in a fragrant white wine broth with garlic, shallots, and butter. The key to success is properly purging the mussels in salted ice water to remove grit, then cooking them quickly in a flavorful base finished with cold butter for a silky, luxurious sauce. Perfect served with crusty bread for dipping. Serves 1 as an entrée or 2 as an appetizer.

times.yield: Serves 1 as a main, 2 as an appetizer

items.name: Dry white wine
items.amount: Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Grigio, or unoaked Chardonnay (100g / scant ½ cup)

steps.text: Dissolve 60g salt in 1500g water with 500g ice in a large container
steps.md: Dissolve 60g salt in 1500g water with 500g ice in a large container

steps.text: Add mussels and refrigerate for 30 minutes to purge grit
steps.md: Add mussels and refrigerate for 30 minutes to purge grit

steps.text: Remove mussels, wipe clean with paper towel, and pull off beards (fibrous strands on flat side) by tugging toward the hinge
steps.md: Remove mussels, wipe clean with paper towel, and pull off beards (fibrous strands on flat side) by tugging toward the hinge

steps.text: Discard any mussels that won't close when squeezed or have cracked shells

steps.text: Keep refrigerated until ready to cook

steps.text: Add tomato paste, cook 1-2 minutes until fragrant
steps.md: Add tomato paste, cook 1-2 minutes until fragrant

steps.text: Deglaze with white wine, bring to a rapid boil
steps.md: Deglaze with white wine, bring to a rapid boil

steps.text: Add mussels, cover, and steam on high heat for 2½-3 minutes
steps.md: Add mussels, cover, and steam on high heat for 2½-3 minutes

steps.text: Remove lid—most shells should be open
steps.md: Remove lid—most shells should be open

steps.text: Reduce heat to low, add cold butter pieces
steps.md: Reduce heat to low, add cold butter pieces

steps.text: Swirl pan until butter emulsifies into a silky broth
steps.md: Swirl pan until butter emulsifies into a silky broth

steps.text: Taste and adjust salt as needed
steps.md: Taste and adjust salt as needed

steps.text: Stir in chopped parsley
steps.md: Stir in chopped parsley

steps.text: Discard any mussels that remain fully closed
steps.md: Discard any mussels that remain fully closed

steps.text: Transfer mussels to a bowl with openings facing up
steps.md: Transfer mussels to a bowl with openings facing up

steps.text: Pour broth over mussels
steps.md: Pour broth over mussels

steps.text: Drizzle with olive oil if desired
steps.md: Drizzle with olive oil if desired

steps.text: Serve immediately with warm crusty bread
steps.md: Serve immediately with warm crusty bread

extras.heading: Tips
extras.md:
- Don't skip the purge—it removes 90-95% of grit
- Keep mussels cold at all times until cooking
- Don't reduce the wine too much; preserve that fresh wine flavor
- Mussels are more forgiving than you think—slightly overcooked is better than undercooked
- Recipe scales easily to 2-3 lbs using a larger Dutch oven
